content.text: I’ll use the knob’s push button and a small screen. Press to start, wait for “GO!”, then press again to see your reaction time. Early presses count as false starts. This needs custom game firmware.

nets.name: +3V3
nets.why: The USB-powered controller supplies 3.3 V to the screen and encoder.

nets.name: GND
nets.why: All modules share the controller ground reference.

nets.name: I2C_SCL
nets.why: GPIO22 clocks screen updates over I2C.

nets.name: I2C_SDA
nets.why: GPIO21 exchanges display data over I2C.

nets.name: BUTTON
nets.why: GPIO25 reads the active-low push button with its internal pull-up enabled.

nets.name: ENCODER_DT
nets.why: GPIO26 connects the encoder data output although rotation is unused in the game.

nets.name: ENCODER_CLK
nets.why: GPIO27 connects the encoder clock output although rotation is unused in the game.

notes.text: Power the controller through USB only; all connected modules use 3.3 V.
Enable the internal pull-up on GPIO25 for the encoder push button.
Check the OLED address on the real module; it is usually 0x3C and sometimes 0x3D.
Reaction times are game estimates, not calibrated measurements; screen refresh and button timing add uncertainty.

behavior.label: Random wait
behavior.value: 2–5 s before the visual GO cue

behavior.label: Button debounce
behavior.value: 20 ms stable release before another press can be accepted

behavior.label: Response timeout
behavior.value: 10 s after GO before showing no response

input.summary: A USB-powered reaction-time game with a screen and a push button that shows your response time and catches false starts.
input.custom_firmware: Implement a visual reaction-time game, not the fixed focus timer. Use SSD1306 128x64 I2C on SDA GPIO21 and SCL GPIO22, auto-detect 0x3C then 0x3D. KY-040 push switch on GPIO25 is active-low with INPUT_PULLUP; configure GPIO26/27 as encoder inputs but ignore rotation. Show 'Press to start' at boot. A new button press starts a round; require button release stable for 20 ms before arming the waiting phase, so holding the start button cannot trigger a response. Display 'Wait...' and choose a fresh random delay uniformly from 2000 to 5000 ms using the ESP32 random source. Any falling edge during this waiting phase is a false start; display 'Too soon!' and offer another round after release. At expiry, display a large 'GO!' and begin reaction timing at completion of the cue's I2C transfer, using a monotonic microsecond clock. Capture the first button falling edge with a GPIO interrupt and timestamp it promptly, including while screen transfers run; do not delay timestamping for debounce. Handle captured edges at the cue boundary consistently, treating edges before cue transfer completion as false starts. Ignore subsequent switch bounce until released continuously for 20 ms. On a valid response display elapsed time rounded to integer milliseconds and session best valid result. If there is no response within 10 s, display 'No response' without updating best. Results remain visible until a fresh press starts the next round after stable release. Do not block button capture with display updates. Rotation has no effect. Keep all game state in RAM; no networking or persistent storage. Results are approximate because of OLED refresh latency and switch timing.

input.summary: The firmware runs a visual reaction-time game with interrupt-timestamped button presses, randomized waits, false-start detection, a ten-second timeout, and a RAM-only session best.
